title.en: Egungun, the Masked One from Deadland
title.zh: 埃貢貢——自冥土歸來的假面

region.en: Yoruba town streets (symbolic pin: festival streets of a Yoruba town near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴城鎮街衢（象徵定位：伊費近郊慶典街道）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Egungun — the word means bone, skeleton — is supposed to be a man risen from the dead, robed in grass and masked in wood, who returns to the land of the living to see what goes on and to carry away the troublesome. To touch him is death; days after a funeral he calls the deceased by name through the night streets, and then brings the family news from Deadland — usually that the dead arrived safely and is well — receiving in return a hidden feast and messages for the departed.
summary.zh: 埃貢貢，本義為「骨」，相傳是死而復返之人：身披草衣、面覆木雕，自冥土回來察看生者世界，專收擾鄰不安之人。觸之即死。葬禮數日後，他率蒙面隨從夜巡街市，高呼亡者之名；再數日，他到喪家報信——亡者已安抵冥土、一切安好。家人備下酒食退出房間（見其進食者死），再託他捎信給逝者。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Egungun masquerade remains a central ancestral institution (also carried into the diaspora and Freetown). Ellis 1894 describes the rite; presented as archival record, not as an insider account.

passages.text: Egungun really means bone, hence skeleton, and Egungun himself is supposed to be a man risen from the dead, acted by a man disguised in a long robe, usually made of grass, and a mask of wood representing a hideous human face, or sometimes the head of an animal. He appears in the streets by day or night, leaping, dancing, or walking grotesquely, and uttering loud cries. He is supposed to have returned from the land of the dead in order to ascertain what is going on in the land of the living, and his function is to carry away those persons who are troublesome to their neighbours — a kind of supernatural inquisitor into the general domestic conduct of people, particularly of women.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Although it is very well known that Egungun is only a disguised man, it is popularly believed that to touch him, even by accident, causes death; to raise the hand against him is punished with death, and women are forbidden, on pain of death, to laugh at him or say he is not one who has risen from the dead. In June there is an annual feast for Egungun lasting seven days, during which lamentations are made for those who have died within the last few years — a kind of All-Souls festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Egungun also appears in connection with funeral ceremonies. A few days after the funeral an Egungun, accompanied by masked and disguised men, parades the streets of the town at night, and, as in the Roman conclamatio, calls upon the deceased loudly by name, a half-frightened crowd following and listening for any response. A few days later he proceeds to the house in which the death took place and brings to the relatives news of the deceased, usually that he has arrived in Deadland safely and is quite well. In return the family set food, rum, and palm-wine in a room of the house and, inviting Egungun to partake, themselves retire — for to see Egungun eating is death. When he and his followers have consumed everything, loud groans are heard from the room, a sign that he is about to depart; the family re-enter and entrust him with messages for the deceased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Oro and the Bull-Roarer That Women Must Not See
title.zh: 奧羅與婦人不得目睹的呼嘯板

region.en: Ondo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: Oro's forest edge outside the town)
region.zh: 奈及利亞翁多城（象徵定位：奧羅巡行的城外林緣）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Oro — fierceness, tempest — is personified executive power, haunting the forest near towns, his approach known by a strange whirring roar made by whirling a thin strip of wood: the bull-roarer, known also to the mysteries of Ancient Greece and Australia. No woman may see the instrument and live; criminals given to Oro are never seen again, their clothes found entangled in a lofty tree.
summary.zh: 「奧羅」意為烈性、風暴，是執行權力的化身，盤踞城鎮近郊的樹林；他的到來以奇異的呼嘯聲為號——那是旋轉薄木片所發的聲響，與古希臘秘儀及澳洲部落所用的「牛吼板」同源。婦女見此物者死。被判交予奧羅的罪犯從此消失，只在參天樹梢尋得纏繞的衣物——人已被他於半空吞噬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Oro society rites are restricted and still practiced; Ellis's 1894 description of secret instruments is presented as an outsider ethnographic record. Restricted rites themselves are not described here beyond what Ellis published.

passages.text: The word Oro means fierceness, tempest, or provocation, and Oro himself appears to be personified executive power. He is supposed to haunt the forest in the neighbourhood of towns, and he makes his approach known by a strange, whirring, roaring noise. As soon as this is heard, all women must shut themselves up in their houses and refrain from looking out on pain of death. The voice of Oro is produced by whirling round and round a thin strip of wood fastened to a stick by a long string — the instrument known to English boys as the bull-roarer, which has been shown to have been used in the mysteries of Ancient Greece, Australia, New Mexico, New Zealand, and South Africa. No women may see the bull-roarer and live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Yoruba country Oro is manipulated by the Ogboni Society. Criminals condemned to death are sometimes given to Oro, in which case they are ordinarily never seen again, but their clothes are shown entangled in the branches of a lofty tree, where Oro is said to have left them when flying through the air; in such a case Oro is said to have devoured the bodies. Unlike Egungun, Oro only appears on his feast-days, when the voice of Oro is heard from morning to night, all women closely confined to their houses, while Oro himself, in a long robe hung with shells and a wooden mask painted white, with the lips smeared with blood, parades the town with a numerous following. In Ondo there is an annual festival to Oro lasting three lunar months; and a large boulder of granite called Olumo, on the summit of a hill in Abeokuta, is sacred to Oro, and no one may ascend it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Abiku: The Hungry Spirits Who Kill Children
title.zh: 阿比庫——奪走孩童的飢靈

region.en: Yoruba bush (symbolic pin: uninhabited tracts where the Abiku dwell, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴荒野（象徵定位：伊費近郊無人居處，阿比庫所棲）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: The empty bush swarms with hungry Abiku spirits who enter the bodies of new-born babes and live on their food, sharing it with the comrades outside until the child pines and dies. Mothers fight back with iron: rings and bells on the ankles, chains on the neck, peppers cut into the flesh to burn the indwelling spirit — and a dead child, buried without ceremony in the bush, may be beaten and mutilated so the Abiku feels every blow and fears to return.
summary.zh: 空曠的野地擠滿飢餓的阿比庫之靈，他們鑽入新生嬰兒體內，奪其食糧，還要與體外的同夥分食，孩子日漸枯瘦而死。母親以鐵相抗：足踝繫鐵環銅鈴、頸掛鐵鏈，甚至以尖椒割入兒身灼燒體內之靈。若孩子夭亡，屍身無葬儀、棄於野，甚或被擊打毀損——阿比庫身受其痛，心生畏懼，不敢再入這位母親日後的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Abiku belief inspired the modern Yoruba novels of Wole Soyinka (The Interpreters imagery) and J. P. Clark's poem Abiku. Descriptions of painful folk remedies reported as 1894 ethnography; handled without endorsement.

passages.text: Abiku means predestined to death, and is used to mean the spirits of children who die before reaching puberty, and also a class of evil spirits who cause children to die. The general idea is that the uninhabited tracts of country abound with evil spirits who suffer from hunger, thirst, and cold, since nobody offers sacrifice to them, and who are constantly endeavouring to improve their condition by entering the bodies of new-born babes. Only one Abiku can enter and dwell in the body of the same child; as there is great competition for such a position, an Abiku is only suffered to enter peaceably on condition of his promising his companions a share of the comforts he is about to obtain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When an Abiku has entered a child he takes for his own use, and for the use of his companions, the greater part of the food that the child eats, who in consequence begins to pine away. It is the incessant demands made by the hungry Abikus outside which destroy the child; when a child is peevish and fretful it is believed that the outside Abikus are hurting him to make the indwelling Abiku give them more to eat. A mother who sees her child wasting away concludes that she has given birth to an Abiku.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: To get rid of the indwelling Abiku and his companions, the anxious mother offers a sacrifice of food and, while the Abikus are supposed to be devouring its spiritual part, attaches iron rings and small bells to the ankles of the child and hangs iron chains round his neck — the jingling keeping the Abikus at a distance, hence the number of children seen with their feet weighed down with iron. If the child grows worse, the mother endeavours to drive out the Abiku by making small incisions in the child's body and putting green peppers or spices in them, believing she thereby causes pain to the Abiku and makes him depart; the poor child screams, but the mother hardens her heart in the belief that the Abiku is suffering equally. Should the child die, it is buried without ceremony in the bush; sometimes the corpse is beaten, pounded, and mutilated while threats and curses are invoked upon the Abiku, who is believed to feel every blow and to be terrified by the threats, so that he fears to enter the body of any other infant the mother may bear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Tree-Spirits: The Ashorin Lure and the Glowing Apa
title.zh: 樹靈：阿紹林之餌與夜光的阿帕樹

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: timber groves near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊伐木林地）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: Several trees are inhabited by spirits, hamadryads rather than gods. The woodman who would fell an Ashorin sets out palm-oil as a lure and cuts while the spirit licks it up. The Apa, African mahogany, is an evil spirit's tree, glowing phosphorescent by night, propitiated with a fowl before its drum-wood may be cut, and by night the haunt of wizards in owl-form. The Iroko silk-cotton tree needs only that the feller rub palm-oil on his own forehead, invoking the spirit of his own head.
summary.zh: 多種大樹內棲樹靈——似古希臘的樹仙女而非大神。伐阿紹林樹者須先在地上抹棕櫚油為餌，趁樹靈舔油時下斧。非洲桃花心木「阿帕」則棲惡靈，夜發磷光，伐其鼓木前須以雞祭之；而巫者夜聚，亦化為貓頭鷹聚於此樹之下。伐伊羅科木棉者，只須以油抹額，喚起自家「頭靈」即可無恙。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; tree-spirit beliefs and woodcutter rites recorded 1894.

passages.text: Several varieties of trees are believed to be inhabited by indwelling spirits, which are not exactly gods, but answer more to the hamadryads of Ancient Greece, or to the elves of mediaeval Europe. The Ashorin tree is one which is inhabited by a spirit who, it is believed, would, if its attention were not diverted, drive away anyone who attempted to fell the tree. The woodman therefore places a little palm-oil on the ground as a lure, and when the spirit leaves the tree to lick up the delicacy, proceeds to cut down its late abode.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Apa, frequently called the African mahogany, is inhabited by an evil spirit, and is commonly seen encircled with palm-leaves, with an earthen pot at its foot to receive the offerings of woodcutters. It is believed to emit a phosphorescent light by night. Before it can be cut down the spirit must be propitiated by an offering, usually a fowl and some palm-oil; the Apa is the emblem of vengeance. The Iroko (silk-cotton tree) is also inhabited by a spirit, but not a powerful or malicious one, and when a man desires to fell such a tree it is sufficient protection for him to invoke the indwelling spirit of his own head by rubbing a little palm-oil on his forehead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wizards and witches are by the Yorubas believed to hold nocturnal meetings at the foot of trees tenanted by spirits, more especially the Apa, whose indwelling spirit is believed to assist them in their malpractices. Here, too, the owl again appears; instead of being the messenger of the tree spirit, it is the witch himself or herself who metamorphoses into an owl and proceeds on the mission of death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Bola's Baby of Otta: The Spirit Who Grew at Market-Time
title.zh: 奧塔的博拉之子——赴市而長的精靈

region.en: Otta, Nigeria (village on the River Ilo, near the Ogun)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧塔村（伊洛河畔，近奧貢河）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: At Otta, a woman named Bola leaves her baby fastened in the house and finds on every market-day that the food has vanished — though the door was never opened. A neighbour demands repayment of cowries the child borrowed, insisting she saw him grown to the size of a ten-year-old. The father hides and watches the baby stand, swell into a big boy, and begin to eat — springing back to infancy at the sight of him. Parents beat the child to drive out the possessing spirit, and the spirit fled.
summary.zh: 奧塔村的博拉每次鎖門赴市，歸來總發現家中食物被吃光，門閂卻分毫未動。鄰婦上門討債——「你的孩子以你的名義借了我的貝幣」，並說來借錢的孩子約莫十歲模樣，比眼前的嬰兒大得多。夫親藏身屋內窺探：只見嬰孩站起，長成大男孩，正要取食——被父親當場撞破，瞬間縮回嬰兒啼哭。父母鞭打驅靈，精靈終於遁去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Ellis notes this is the Yoruba counterpart of the European changeling — a strong cross-tradition parallel for the Compare view. Cross-refs: none recorded in corpus for changeling; closest thematic relative is the Abiku cycle.

passages.text: There lived at Otta, a village on the River Ilo, a woman named Bola, who had a male child. When the child was small the mother carried him on her back to market, but when he was about nine months old she used to lay him on a mat in her house, fasten the door, and go to market by herself. After this it always happened that when she returned from market she found that all the food she had left in the house had disappeared — though the door-fastening was always untouched. One day a neighbour came to demand repayment of the string of cowries that Bola had sent her little boy to borrow; Bola protested that the child was too young to walk or talk, but the neighbour, looking closely at the sleeping child, solemnly declared that it was really he who had come to her — though when he came he was much bigger, with the appearance of a child of about ten years of age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Bola heard this she was much distressed, fearing her child was possessed by an evil spirit; she paid the cowries and begged the neighbour to say nothing, then told her husband the whole story. The father hid himself in the house one day while mother and child were out; scarcely had Bola gone and fastened the door than the father saw the baby stand up and begin to grow till he became a big boy, going to the calabashes where the food was kept and beginning to eat. Immediately the child saw his father he became a little baby again and lay on the floor crying. He was possessed by a spirit. His mother came back, and they beat him to drive the spirit out, so that the spirit fled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man-Hyena of the Night Forest

region.en: Yoruba night-forest (symbolic pin: dark paths beyond the town, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴夜林（象徵定位：伊費城外夜路）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: The hyena is often supposed to be a man who assumes that disguise at night to prey upon sheep and cattle — and, if the opportunity offers, upon human beings. Such man-hyenas can, by certain howls and cries, compel people to come out to them in the dark forest to be devoured; the weird laugh of the hyena and its nocturnal habits account for the belief.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人常謂鬣狗實為夜間易形之人，白日為人，夜著獸形，捕食羊牛——有機可乘時，也吃人。這種人形鬣狗能以特殊嚎叫與呼喚，逼人深夜走進黑暗的樹林任其吞噬。鬣狗那怪異的「笑聲」與夜行習性，正是此一信念的根源。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; were-hyena belief, the African analogue of the werewolf, recorded 1894 (cf. Abyssinia).

passages.text: We also find a superstition which recalls that of the were-wolf, for the hyena is often supposed to be a man who assumes that disguise at night, to prey upon sheep and cattle, and, if the opportunity offers, upon human beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Such man-hyenas are believed to be able, by means of certain howls and cries, to compel people to go out to them in the dark forest to be devoured. A similar belief is found in Abyssinia. The weird laugh of the hyena, and its nocturnal habits, no doubt account for this superstition, just as similar causes have led to the owl being universally regarded as a bird of ill omen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Iyewa Becomes a Lagoon to Save Her Children

region.en: Odo Iyewa lagoon, Nigeria (the water named for the mother)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊耶瓦潟湖（以母親之名為名的水域）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VI

summary.en: A poor woman, Iyewa, gathered firewood daily with her two children; one day, deep in the forest, they lost the path, and, tormented with thirst, the children cried for water until they lay near death. Prostrating herself, Iyewa called upon the gods, who changed her into a lagoon at which the children drank and recovered. When they grew up they built their house beside the water and named it Odo Iyewa — the Lagoon of Iyewa.
summary.zh: 貧婦伊耶瓦日日攜二子入林拾柴換糧。某日迷途林中，孩子渴極哀號，氣息奄奄。她伏地呼神求救；眾神應允，將她化作一泓潟湖。孩子俯身痛飲，得救生還。二人成年後在水畔築屋，命名「伊耶瓦之湖」，永誌其母。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; metamorphosis-and-place-name legend recorded 1894. The Iyewa lagoon lies near the Badagry creek country.

passages.text: The Iyewa lagoon is also said to have been a woman. A poor woman, named Iyewa, had two children whom she had a hard struggle to support; but she used every day to go with them into the forest to gather firewood, which she carried to the town and sold for food. One day, finding wood scarce, she and the children wandered further into the forest than usual, and when it was time to return they could not find their way out. They walked hither and thither looking for the path, but in vain, and at last, tired out and tormented with thirst, they lay down to rest under a large tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: This rested their limbs, but their thirst increased, and the two children filled the forest with their lamentations, crying to their mother for water. The poor woman, half distracted, sprang to her feet and again searched in every direction for the path and for water, but fruitlessly; and when at last she returned to her children she found them almost at the last gasp. Then, prostrating herself upon the earth, she called upon the gods to come to her assistance and save her children. The gods listened to her prayer, and Iyewa was at once changed into a lagoon, at which the children drank and so recovered; while next day they were found by neighbours and taken back to the town. When the children grew up they built a house by the side of the lagoon, which, in memory of their mother, they called Odo Iyewa — the Lagoon of Iyewa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VI (1894); not verbatim.
